question: Cast iron vs non-stick pan for everyday cooking: which is better for health, which lasts longer, and is it true scratched non-stick is toxic?
reference:
Health: both are safe when used properly. Non-stick (PTFE/Teflon) is chemically inert; swallowed flakes pass straight through you. The real risks are overheating (an empty pan above about 260 C / 500 F gives off fumes that cause flu-like "polymer fume fever" and can kill pet birds) and the old manufacturing aid PFOA, phased out of US production by 2015 and banned in the EU in 2020. Current pans are "PFOA-free" but PTFE is itself a PFAS, which is why Minnesota banned PFAS cookware sales from 2025 and the EU is weighing a restriction.

Scratched non-stick: not acutely toxic, but a 2022 Flinders/Newcastle study estimated a single scratch sheds about 9,100 microplastic particles and a broken coating about 2.3 million. Long-term effects of ingested PTFE particles are unproven, so the standard advice is: once it is flaking or deeply scratched, replace it.

Cast iron: no coating, adds a little dietary iron (fine for most, a caution for haemochromatosis), handles any heat, but is heavy, needs seasoning, rusts if left wet, and dislikes long simmers of acidic food.

Lifespan: non-stick lasts 2 to 5 years with care (wood or silicone tools, medium heat, no dishwasher, no metal scourers). Cast iron lasts generations.

Verdict: cast iron (or carbon steel/stainless) for everyday searing and longevity; keep one cheap non-stick for eggs and fish at low-medium heat, and bin it when it scratches.

Construction started 28 January 1887 and finished 31 March 1889 (2 years, 2 months), by Gustave Eiffel's company for the 1889 Exposition Universelle marking the centenary of the French Revolution. It opened to the public on 15 May 1889.

Height: 300 m (984 ft) to the top of the structure; 330 m (1,083 ft) to the tip of the antennas since a new digital-radio antenna was added in March 2022 (it was 324 m before that). About 7,300 tonnes of wrought iron, 10,100 tonnes in total, with 18,038 iron parts and 2.5 million rivets.

Temporary: Eiffel's permit let him keep the ticket income for 20 years, after which the tower would pass to the City of Paris, which planned to dismantle it in 1909. Many Paris artists had petitioned against the "useless and monstrous" tower. It survived because Eiffel made it useful for science and the military: from 1898 he funded wireless-telegraphy experiments from the top, the army installed a permanent radio station in 1903-1908, and in 1910 the city renewed the concession. It then served as a transmitter for time signals and later radio and TV. It now draws about 6 to 7 million visitors a year.

question: how does general anaesthetic work? like how does it knock you out and stop you remembering anything, and why do they tell you not to eat before
reference:
A general anaesthetic is a cocktail, not one drug. Propofol into a vein puts you under; an inhaled gas such as sevoflurane (or more propofol) keeps you there. These drugs boost GABA-A receptors, the brain's main inhibitory "brake", and some (ketamine, nitrous oxide) also block the excitatory NMDA receptor. The cortex is damped and the thalamus and brain regions stop communicating in a coordinated way, so integrated consciousness switches off. It is closer to a reversible, controlled coma than sleep, which is why an anaesthetist monitors your breathing, heart and drug levels throughout.

Memory goes first. The hippocampus, which writes new memories, is extremely sensitive to these drugs (and to midazolam, often given beforehand). At doses lower than those needed to knock you out, new memories simply are not encoded, so there is nothing to recall; old memories are untouched. Pain is handled separately with opioids and local anaesthetic, and a muscle relaxant is often added for the breathing tube.

Fasting is about your lungs. Anaesthesia switches off the gag and cough reflexes and relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach, so stomach contents can flow back up and into the lungs, causing aspiration pneumonitis, which can be fatal. Current rules (ASA, UK and European societies): no solid food for 6 hours (8 hours after a fatty or fried meal), breast milk 4 hours, but clear fluids such as water, black coffee or pulp-free juice are allowed up to 2 hours before and are encouraged. Tell the team if you take a GLP-1 drug such as Ozempic or Wegovy; those slow stomach emptying and may need a longer fast.

question: Airbus A380 vs Boeing 747: which is bigger, how many passengers does each carry and why did they stop making both?
reference:
The A380 is the bigger aircraft by almost every measure; the 747 is only slightly longer.

Size (A380-800 vs 747-8): length 72.7 m vs 76.3 m; wingspan 79.8 m vs 68.4 m; height 24.1 m vs 19.4 m; max take-off weight 575 t vs about 448 t. The A380's full-length double deck gives it roughly 40% more cabin floor area than the 747-8.

Passengers: A380 typically 500-550 in three or four classes (Airbus reference layout 525; Emirates' densest 615), certified maximum 853 all-economy. 747-8 Intercontinental typically about 400-410 in three classes (Lufthansa flies 364), exit limit 605. The older 747-400 carried about 416 typically, up to 660.

Why both ended: airlines switched to big twin-engine jets (777, 787, A350) that burn far less fuel per seat, have two engines to maintain instead of four, and can fly long point-to-point routes profitably instead of funnelling 500+ passengers through a hub. The A380 won only 251 orders (254 built including test aircraft) against a roughly $25 billion development cost; when Emirates cut 39 orders in February 2019 Airbus announced the end, and the last A380 went to Emirates on 16 December 2021. It had no freighter version to fall back on. The 747 lived longer because of its nose-loading freighter: passenger 747-8 sales were tiny (about 48), freighter orders eventually dried up too, and Boeing delivered the last 747, a 747-8F to Atlas Air, on 31 January 2023 after 1,574 built over 54 years. question: why does a bike stay upright when its moving but falls over the second it stops
reference:
A moving bike stays up because it can steer; a stopped bike cannot. Upright, a bike is an inverted pendulum: once it starts to lean it falls, and nothing stops that when the wheels are not rolling. While rolling, the front wheel automatically turns toward whichever side the bike leans, which steers the tyres back under the centre of mass and straightens it up. You do the same thing unconsciously when riding: to stay upright you steer into the fall.

Three things make the front wheel turn into a lean by itself:
- Trail (caster): the steering axis meets the ground ahead of the tyre's contact patch, so a lean makes the ground push the wheel into the turn, like a shopping-trolley wheel following the push.
- Gyroscopic precession: a leaning torque on the spinning front wheel makes it turn toward the lean.
- Front-end mass: the handlebars and fork sit ahead of the steering axis, so they fall into the lean and drag the wheel round.

The classic "gyroscope holds it up" story is wrong on its own: bike wheels are too light and slow. In 2011 Cornell and TU Delft researchers (Kooijman et al., Science) built a bike with counter-rotating wheels (no gyro effect) and negative trail that still balanced itself. The essential ingredient is any geometry that couples leaning to steering.

Self-stability only works in a speed band (roughly 14-30 km/h for a normal bike); slower, the rider must steer actively; at zero speed no steering input moves the contact patches, so it falls.

This is almost certainly decompression sickness (the bends), possibly with arterial gas embolism from the fast ascent. Shoulder pain, dizziness and arm tingling within an hour of a rapid ascent are classic. Treat it as an emergency; he needs a recompression (hyperbaric) chamber.

2. Put him on 100% oxygen from the boat's emergency kit (demand valve or non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min) and keep it going until it runs out or medics take over, even if he feels better.

question: Why did Concorde stop flying? How fast did it go, why did it never make money, and is anyone seriously bringing supersonic passenger flights back?

Speed: Concorde cruised at Mach 2.04, about 2,180 km/h (1,350 mph) at 55,000-60,000 ft, flying London-New York in about 3.5 hours versus 7-8 on a 747. It carried 100 passengers and flew 1976-2003.

question: how does a microwave actually heat food, and why does it heat the edges but leave the middle of my leftovers cold. also why cant you put metal in it
reference:
How it heats: a magnetron makes radio waves at 2.45 GHz. The electric field flips direction about 2.45 billion times a second, and polar molecules in the food (mainly water, also fats and sugars) try to keep turning to follow it. That rotation and the collisions it causes generate heat throughout the outer layer of the food (dielectric heating). It is not a "resonance" with water, just a frequency water absorbs well and that is free to use.

Why the middle stays cold: the waves do not go all the way through. In wet food they are mostly absorbed in the outer 1-3 cm, so anything thicker than that heats only on the outside and the centre has to warm by slow conduction. Edges and corners get hit from several sides at once, so they heat fastest. The oven also has standing-wave hot and cold spots a few centimetres apart (the turntable only partly evens this out), and frozen parts absorb far less than thawed parts, so warm spots run away while icy spots lag. Fixes: spread food in a ring with a hole in the middle, stir halfway, cover it, use medium power for longer, and let it stand 1-2 minutes.

Metal: metal reflects microwaves instead of absorbing them. On thin or sharp metal (fork tines, crumpled foil, gold rims) the field concentrates, builds thousands of volts and sparks across the air (arcing), which can scorch the oven, ignite food or damage the magnetron, especially with little food to absorb the energy. The oven's own walls are smooth metal and are fine; a smooth spoon in a mug usually is too, but makers say avoid it.

Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62 in the Valley of the Kings, Luxor) was found by the British archaeologist Howard Carter, funded by George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon. It is the only near-intact royal tomb ever found in Egypt. Carter spent about ten years cataloguing its roughly 5,000 objects. Tutankhamun died young, at about 18 or 19, around 1323 BC. He became pharaoh at roughly age 9 and reigned for about nine or ten years during Egypt's 18th Dynasty. question: How does carbon dating work and why can't it be used on dinosaur bones?
reference:
Carbon-14 is a radioactive form of carbon made constantly in the upper atmosphere when cosmic rays hit nitrogen-14. It mixes into CO2, so every living plant and animal carries about the same tiny ratio of C-14 to normal C-12 (about one atom in a trillion). When something dies it stops taking in carbon, and its C-14 decays back to nitrogen with a half-life of 5,730 years. Labs (usually with an accelerator mass spectrometer) measure how much C-14 is left: half remaining means about 5,730 years, a quarter about 11,460, and so on. The raw result is corrected with a calibration curve (IntCal20) built from tree rings, corals and cave deposits, because atmospheric C-14 has varied over time.

Why not dinosaurs: after about 50,000 years (8 to 9 half-lives) less than 0.1% of the original C-14 remains, which is too little to tell from background contamination, so the practical limit is roughly 50,000 to 55,000 years. The last non-bird dinosaurs died 66 million years ago, more than 11,000 half-lives, so every original C-14 atom is gone. Fossil bone is also mineralised, with the original carbon largely replaced by rock. Dinosaurs are dated instead with long-lived isotopes in volcanic layers above and below the fossils: uranium-lead (half-life 4.5 billion years) and potassium-argon or argon-argon (1.25 billion years), which work on millions-of-years timescales.

question: What happened in the Great Smog of London in 1952? How many people died, what caused it and what laws came out of it?

What happened: from Friday 5 to Tuesday 9 December 1952 a thick yellow-black smog sat over London. Visibility fell to a metre or less in places; buses, trains and ambulances stopped (only the Underground ran), cinemas and theatres closed because audiences couldn't see the screen, and prize cattle at Smithfield show suffocated. Hospitals filled with people with bronchitis, pneumonia and heart failure.

Deaths: the government's figure at the time was about 4,000 excess deaths in the first weeks, mostly elderly people and those with heart and lung disease. Deaths stayed high for months; a 2004 analysis puts the total at around 12,000, with over 100,000 made ill. That makes it the deadliest air-pollution event in British history.

Causes: a stationary anticyclone brought cold, windless weather and a temperature inversion - a lid of warm air trapping cold air at ground level. The cold made Londoners burn more coal, and much of it was cheap high-sulphur "nutty slack" because the best coal was exported to earn foreign currency. Get it looked at this week. A mole that has changed colour (darker) and developed an uneven edge hits two of the main warning signs, and "someone else noticed a change" is exactly how melanomas get caught. It does not mean it is cancer (most changed moles are benign), but change is the single most important sign and only a doctor with a dermatoscope can tell.

The ABCDE check:
- Asymmetry: one half unlike the other.
- Border: ragged, notched or blurred edge (yours).
- Colour: uneven, several shades of brown/black, or new black, blue, red or white areas, or getting darker (yours).
- Diameter: over 6 mm (pencil eraser), though melanomas can be smaller.
- Evolving: any change in size, shape, colour or height, or itching, bleeding, crusting, soreness (yours).
Also the "ugly duckling" sign: a mole that looks different from all your others.

What to do:
1. Take a clear photo now next to a ruler or coin, so change can be tracked.
2. Book a GP or dermatologist appointment and say "changing mole". In the UK a GP will make an urgent 2-week-wait skin cancer referral if it looks suspicious. In the US ask a dermatologist for a prompt appointment.
3. Do not pick at it or wait for it to bleed.
4. The usual next step is removal under local anaesthetic (excision biopsy), 20-30 minutes, then lab results in 1-3 weeks.

Caught early (stage 1), melanoma has around a 98-99% five-year survival; the back is a common site because people cannot see it themselves, so your partner did the right thing.

question: What's a normal blood pressure for an adult? Mine was 138 over 88 at the pharmacy machine. Is that high and should I do anything about it?

Normal for an adult is under 120/80. Your 138/88 is above normal, but the label depends on where you live. Under the US ACC/AHA guideline (2017, reaffirmed August 2025) 130-139 over 80-89 is "stage 1 hypertension". In the UK, NHS/NICE only call it high blood pressure at 140/90 in a clinic (135/85 average at home), so 138/88 is "high-normal"; the European Society of Cardiology (2024) calls 120-139/70-89 "elevated". ### What is CPR?

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is used when a person's heart has stopped beating, called cardiac arrest, or when a person has stopped breathing. CPR is an emergency technique that keeps blood and oxygen moving through the body until emergency medical help arrives.

When someone's heart stops or they stop breathing, every second matters. Without treatment, permanent brain damage can happen quickly. If you know how to perform CPR, you could save a life.

### How is CPR done?

The steps below give you a general overview of CPR. Reading about CPR is not the same as hands-on training. Taking an accredited course is the best way to be prepared in an emergency.

Before starting CPR, check the person. Tap their shoulder and shout, "Are you okay?" Look to see if they are breathing normally. Gasping or gurgling is not normal breathing. If they do not respond and are not breathing normally, start the steps below right away.

Call 911. If someone else is nearby, send them to call while you start CPR.

Send someone to find an AED. An automated external defibrillator (AED) is a device that can shock the heart back into a normal rhythm. It gives you step-by-step voice instructions. AEDs are especially useful in sudden cardiac arrest, when the heart stops unexpectedly due to an electrical problem. AEDs are available in many public places.

Position the person. Make sure that the person is lying on their back. Start CPR right away. Do not wait to move them to a different surface.

Start chest compressions:

- Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest and place your other hand on top.
- Position your shoulders above your hands, lock your elbows.
- Push straight down, hard and fast to about 2 inches deep.
- Go at a steady pace of about 100 to 120 pushes per minute.
- Let the chest fully rise back up between each push.

If you haven't had any CPR training, you can do hands-only CPR for a teen or adult whose heart has stopped beating. Hands-only CPR uses chest compressions only, with no breaths, to keep blood circulating. Keep pushing until help arrives or the person starts breathing normally.

If you've had CPR training, you can give breaths along with chest compressions. After every 30 compressions:

- Open the airway by tilting the head and lifting the chin.
- Pinch the person's nose shut and give 2 breaths, each lasting about 1 second.
- Watch for the chest to rise.

Use the AED as soon as it is available. Turn the AED on and follow the voice instructions. It will tell you when to stop compressions and when to deliver a shock. Continue CPR right after.

Children need both chest compressions and breaths. Hands-only CPR alone is not recommended for children. Push down about one-third the depth of the child's chest. If an AED has child pads, use them. If not, adult pads may be used.

The steps above are an overview only. To be truly prepared, take an accredited CPR course and refresh your training every two years. Many community organizations, hospitals, the American Heart Association, and the American Red Cross offer classes.

question: Why do leaves turn red and yellow in autumn? Where does the colour come from and why do some trees stay green?
reference:
Leaves are green because of chlorophyll, which does photosynthesis and is constantly rebuilt all summer. Two other sets of pigments make the autumn colours.

Yellow and orange come from carotenoids (xanthophylls and beta-carotene, the same pigments as in carrots and corn). They are in the leaf all year but hidden by the far larger amount of chlorophyll. As nights lengthen in autumn the tree grows a corky abscission layer at the base of each leaf stalk, cutting off water and nutrients. Chlorophyll production stops, the existing chlorophyll breaks down within days, and the yellow that was always there shows through (birch, aspen, hickory, ginkgo).

Red and purple come from anthocyanins, which are made fresh in autumn from sugars trapped in the leaf once the abscission layer forms. Bright sunny days plus cool but frost-free nights produce the most sugar and the brightest reds (red maple, sumac, dogwood, red oak). The tree probably makes them as a sunscreen while it pulls nitrogen and other nutrients back into the branches. Browns, as in oaks and beech, are tannins left after the other pigments break down.

Evergreens (pines, spruces, firs, holly) keep their leaves because the leaves are built for winter: needles or thick waxy leaves with little surface area, sunken pores, and cell fluids rich in sugars and antifreeze proteins that resist freezing and drying. Each needle lives 2 to 7 years or more and is shed a few at a time, so the tree is never bare and keeps its nutrients. Broad thin deciduous leaves would freeze and dry out, so it is cheaper for those trees to reclaim the nutrients and drop them.
